entries.name: Amara
entries.summary: Gives older adults a voice-controlled tablet for family calls, music, and reminders.

scene.job: It gives an older adult a voice-controlled tablet for calls, music, and reminders, while the family manages it from an app.
scene.seller: Adult children and other family members buy the membership.
scene.payer: The family pays privately.

deep_dive.product: Amara Home is a voice-operated tablet that arrives pre-configured. Older adults speak to call family, play radio, hear reminders, and ask questions. Relatives manage setup via a family app. Company page: DSGVO on European servers; membership includes tablet, dock, family app, and content.
deep_dive.how_it_works: 1) Device ships set up. 2) User speaks. 3) Family uses the app for photos, messages, calendar. WLAN or integrated SIM; no smartphone required for the older adult.
deep_dive.user: Older adults living at home (company framing: Oma / Opa).
deep_dive.payer: Private pay / family membership. No SGB XI or DiPA listing found on company page.
deep_dive.business_model: Membership bundling hardware and content. Exact euro list price on the public homepage fetch: not found.
deep_dive.traction: AgeTechX Ones to Watch 2026. Customer quotes dated 2026 on site. Public install counts: not found.
deep_dive.funding: EUR 3.7 million pre-seed; investors Econa, Caesar VC, IBB Ventures (IBB Ventures news). Legal entity H2 Technologies GmbH, founded 2025 by Philipp Hartz and Richard Hector; team about eight (same source).
deep_dive.team: Co-founders Philipp Hartz and Richard Hector (company site; IBB Ventures; AgeTechX speaker page for Hector).
deep_dive.competitors: Senior tablets and senior apps (company table). In our scan: Harmonica/Olympia, inTouch, Zenaris.
deep_dive.regulatory: Consumer / private device. No DiGA or DiPA listing found. Company claims DSGVO / EU servers.
deep_dive.thesis: Interpreted: serves aging adults who will not use a normal tablet; job is connection and light daily structure; seller Amara to the family; payer is the family. Why now: loneliness products sell on affection; DE survey context in T07 shows loneliness is not simply highest at 76+. Kill risk: T07 is kill on the pickable menu; no Kasse path found; crowded check-in shelf.
risks: No named DE payer beyond family cash.
T07 theme is kill on the pickable menu.
Hardware CapEx and churn not published.
deep_dive.relevance: Tied to T07 (social isolation). Standing disposition: kill. Cards T07-H1 and T07-H2 are stressed, still standing as what-ifs, not build permission.
open_questions: Who cancels: older adult or family?

entries.summary: Alerts care staff to change an incontinence product, and can signal movement and falls.

deep_dive.product: alea: sensor strip in incontinence products plus reusable clip; app/web notifies caregivers. Also markets movement, fall detection, and documentation. Health Capital coverage of funding calls alea a certified medical device.
deep_dive.how_it_works: Clip attaches to smart diaper/sensor strip; data to cloud; staff get smartphone/tablet/browser alerts; change when needed rather than fixed rounds only.
deep_dive.user: Residents in care homes (company also mentions outpatient/clinical).
deep_dive.payer: Operator CapEx/OpEx. Shared night workflow is not a default individual GKV Hilfsmittel (T02 continuum). DiPA listing: not found.
deep_dive.business_model: Hardware + SaaS. Public list prices: not found.
deep_dive.traction: Deep Tech Award 2023; Innovation Award Berlin Brandenburg nomination 2025 (Berlin Partner). Brandenburg production plans (Health Capital). Facility install counts: not found on homepage.
deep_dive.funding: EUR 5.2m (Albers Investment, Brandenburg Kapital, Conle; Next Big Thing, IBB Capital) - Health Capital. FinSMEs 25 Aug 2026: EUR 6.5m with CRB Health Tech, Vorwerk Ventures, SUM Ventures and existing investors.
deep_dive.team: Founded 2017 Berlin. Julio Brandl (CEO in funding quotes); Jens Grudno co-founder (Crunchbase/5-HT).
deep_dive.competitors: TENA SmartCare Identifi, Hartmann HILMAS, tilt beds that do not answer skip-or-change (T02 cards).
deep_dive.regulatory: Funding coverage: medical device. DiPA listing: not found. Hilfsmittelverzeichnis positionsnummer for clip: not found this pass.
deep_dive.thesis: Interpreted: care-home incontinence need-based change; seller AssistMe to Betreiber; payer facility. Why now: night continence is the frequent night task (Witten survey on T01/T02). Kill risk: T02 menu kill vs named shelf; Identifi already sells skip-or-change; Betreiber CapEx needs named distribution.
risks: Menu kill on new Heim incontinence workflow.
No published German rate that alea cancels avoidable rounds.
deep_dive.relevance: Adjacent to T02 kill and T02-H1 (stressed still standing). Scouting allowed; designing a rival is not.
open_questions: Outcome vs Identifi in same house?

entries.title: Tuktu
entries.job: Tuktu matches families with local helpers for companionship, rides, housework, shopping, dementia care, and overnight care. The company says helpers are background-checked through Certn, and that a booking can start at one hour with no long contract, on the site, by phone, or in an app. The head office is in Vancouver, and the helper list includes Vancouver, Victoria, Kelowna, Edmonton, and Markham.
entries.who_pays: Families pay by the hour. The site lists companionship at 22 to 30 dollars an hour, help at home at 30 to 40 dollars, and mobility help or dementia and overnight care at 35 to 45 dollars. A question on the same site says services start at 25 dollars an hour. Care homes, non-profits, and retiree groups are offered discounts, with no public rate.

what_it_does.text: Tuktu matches families with local helpers for companionship, rides, housework, shopping, dementia care, and overnight care. The company says helpers are background-checked through Certn, and that a booking can start at one hour with no long contract, on the site, by phone, or in an app. The head office is in Vancouver, and the helper list includes Vancouver, Victoria, Kelowna, Edmonton, and Markham.

who_pays.text: Families pay by the hour. The site lists companionship at 22 to 30 dollars an hour, help at home at 30 to 40 dollars, and mobility help or dementia and overnight care at 35 to 45 dollars. A question on the same site says services start at 25 dollars an hour. Care homes, non-profits, and retiree groups are offered discounts, with no public rate.

traction.text: The company site states 5,000 or more families and caregivers supported, 50,000 or more hours of care, and 600 or more certified caregivers. Those figures are not dated. A New Ventures BC profile from July 2022, after a launch earlier that year, reported over 230 customers and providers, about 150 companions in the Lower Mainland, 60 percent monthly user growth, and a 750,000 dollar pre-seed round. Tuktu Care Inc. was incorporated on 29 January 2019, and the corporation record shows a 2026 annual return.

why_interesting.text: The offer is hourly help without an agency contract, which suits a family that needs a ride or a few hours of company rather than a full care shift. The jump from the July 2022 counts to the much larger figures on the current homepage is wide, and the larger figures are the company's own, with no outside check found.

status.text: The site is taking bookings at a Vancouver head office and a toll-free number. A federal corporation record for Tuktu Care Inc. shows a 2026 annual return with a meeting date of 6 November 2025, and lists Rustam Sengupta as director.

entries.title: Darmiyan
entries.job: Darmiyan's BrainSee is prescription software for doctors. For a person aged 55 to 95 who already has amnestic mild cognitive impairment, it reads a standard brain MRI, age, sex and memory-test scores and returns a score from 0 to 100. A score above 50 looks more like people who developed Alzheimer's dementia within five years, and a score below 50 looks more like people who did not. The FDA says a doctor must not diagnose or decide treatment from this score alone, and the scan needs no contrast dye.
entries.who_pays: Doctors order it. The FDA limits sale and use to prescription, and clinicians upload the MRI through a web portal. No public price is listed.

what_it_does.text: Darmiyan's BrainSee is prescription software for doctors. For a person aged 55 to 95 who already has amnestic mild cognitive impairment, it reads a standard brain MRI, age, sex and memory-test scores and returns a score from 0 to 100. A score above 50 looks more like people who developed Alzheimer's dementia within five years, and a score below 50 looks more like people who did not. The FDA says a doctor must not diagnose or decide treatment from this score alone, and the scan needs no contrast dye.

who_pays.text: Doctors order it. The FDA limits sale and use to prescription, and clinicians upload the MRI through a web portal. No public price is listed.

traction.text: The FDA granted De Novo clearance DEN220066 on 11 January 2024, after a breakthrough designation the company dates to May 2021. In the clearance study, 198 people at 27 North American hospitals were scored against five years of follow-up: specificity was 96.3% and sensitivity was 72.9%. The company said in January 2024 that doctors could use it through a secure web portal. No sales or user count is published.

why_interesting.text: It uses an ordinary MRI a memory clinic may already have, instead of a spinal tap or a PET scan, and it forecasts five years ahead rather than claiming to diagnose Alzheimer's on the spot. The FDA created a new device category for it. The same review notes that the study group was mostly white, that the low end of the sensitivity range sat under the 70% bar the company had set, and that a follow-up study in a wider group of patients was required.

status.text: The company website still presents BrainSee as its first product, with FDA clearance in January 2024. No 2025 or 2026 sales update was found.

entries.claim: What if the children can settle who gets the house by a private contract over the parent's future estate, without the owner and without a Notar.
entries.status_raw: killed (2026-10-04 16:19 Europe/Berlin). § 311b Abs. 4 BGB: "Ein Vertrag über den Nachlass eines noch lebenden Dritten ist nichtig." The same for a contract over the Pflichtteil or a legacy from that estate. Abs. 5 allows a contract among future statutory heirs about the statutory share or Pflichtteil of one of them only with notarial recording. Abs. 1 requires notarial form for a promise to transfer land. A private, unnotarised deal over the living parent's house or estate is void. Dead exploration stays on file. Sibling P01-H1 still stands. No brokerage.

status.text: The London office at 1 Water Lane is on the founder page. Care Talk reported on 15 April 2026 that Cera was launching an AI lab, and the BBC profile of 1 October 2026 still names Ben Maruthappu as founder and chief executive.

traction.text: Dr Ben Maruthappu co-founded Cera in 2016. He is a doctor, previously advised the chief executive of NHS England, and was educated at Oxford, Cambridge, and Harvard. TechCrunch reported on 12 January 2025 that Cera raised 150 million dollars, mostly debt, and had raised more than 407 million dollars in total. The BBC wrote on 1 October 2026 that Cera says it has 13,500 staff and almost 500 million pounds of annual revenue.

who_pays.text: Governments, insurers, and the NHS pay, the mission page says. No public price. A family price was not on the mission page or in the January 2025 TechCrunch report. No reimbursement tariff for a private buyer was found.

what_it_does.text: Cera sends carers and nurses to homes in the UK. Its mission page says the work is for governments, insurers, and the NHS, and that carers log visits so the company can flag risks. TechCrunch reported the notes are used to predict falls and hospital stays.

why_interesting.text: Cera employs the carers, so the warning claims rest on its own visit notes. The BBC figures and the hospital percentages are the company's, and the January 2025 money was mostly debt.

entries.job: Confidant is a phone app from Confidant Technologies in Valencia. A family member can see where an older person's Android phone or watch is, get an alert when they leave or arrive at set places, and start a video call that opens on the other device so they can see and hear what is happening. The same app can lock apps and is also sold for watching children. The older person can wear a watch and does not have to tap the screen.
entries.who_pays: Families pay. In November 2023, founder Jose Rogero told the EFE news agency that one device cost €9.99 a month and five devices cost €19.99 a month, with a free version for basic safety. The live website does not list a price, so those figures may have changed.

what_it_does.text: Confidant is a phone app from Confidant Technologies in Valencia. A family member can see where an older person's Android phone or watch is, get an alert when they leave or arrive at set places, and start a video call that opens on the other device so they can see and hear what is happening. The same app can lock apps and is also sold for watching children. The older person can wear a watch and does not have to tap the screen.

who_pays.text: Families pay. In November 2023, founder Jose Rogero told the EFE news agency that one device cost €9.99 a month and five devices cost €19.99 a month, with a free version for basic safety. The live website does not list a price, so those figures may have changed.

traction.text: EFE reported in November 2023 that the app had thousands of users, mainly in Spain, and also in Mexico and Switzerland. The first paid version launched at Christmas 2018 through the Lanzadera accelerator in Valencia. Google Play still lists the app under Confidant Technologies S.L. in Valencia, last updated on 3 March 2025.

why_interesting.text: Rogero built it after his mother-in-law, who later developed Alzheimer's, stopped answering the phone and the family had to drive over to check she was safe. The check is a video call that opens by itself, and the app can also stop the phone being switched off or put into flight mode. That is a different bargain from a button alarm: the family can look in, and the older person does not have to do anything.

status.text: The website is live and Google Play still distributes the app, with an update dated 3 March 2025. In November 2023 the founder said dedicated phones and a watch, with fall detection, were planned for early 2024. No later page confirmed that those devices went on sale.

The site says pharmacists developed the formulas, the capsules are made in Germany, and buyers can get their money back within 90 days. who_pays.text: Shoppers pay Forward Health GmbH on fortea.de. The imprint names that company as the seller. The pages fetched do not show a price.

traction.text: The shop says its overall rating is 4.6 out of 5 from 4,177 reviews. Individual products show their own counts, including 671 reviews for the joint capsules, and the page shows reviews dated into October 2026.

why_interesting.text: The imprint names Forward Health GmbH of Elisabeth-Treskow-Platz 1, Cologne, as the seller, with managing directors Alexander Thelen and Justus Sander. The register purpose is supplements, and the shop is a consumer capsule brand rather than a care service.

status.text: As of 5 October 2026 the Fortea shop is publishing customer reviews, including some dated 3 October 2026. Northdata shows a shareholder list for Forward Health GmbH dated 14 September 2026.

entries.job: It handles the paperwork of ending and transferring contracts after a death, and notifies the service providers.

total.amount: €1.5 million in July 2022, after €300,000 in November 2018

status.text: The checkout still quotes 97.80 euro, so the service is on sale. No news found in the last 12 months.

traction.text: Chantal van der Velde and Graciëlla van Vliet founded Closure in 2018. Before that, van Vliet worked as a part-time management trainee in China while pursuing a master's in econometrics and machine learning. The July 2022 funding note also spells her surname van Hamersveld. Closure raised 300,000 euro in November 2018 and 1.5 million euro in July 2022 from Borski Fund and Rabobank. It said it worked with more than 200 funeral homes. In January 2023 van Vliet said one in four Dutch deaths was reported through Closure.

who_pays.text: A family on Closure's own checkout pays 97.80 euro. Silicon Canals wrote in January 2023 that the service was free of charge to heirs because companies pay to offer it. Both descriptions are published, and they are not the same model. Funeral directors also refer families.

what_it_does.text: Closure collects one set of details after a death and asks companies to end or transfer the person's contracts, from phone and energy to insurers, charities, and social accounts. The family picks the organisations and tracks each request. A 2022 note says a Dutch financial-markets licence lets it notify banks and insurers.

why_interesting.text: Funeral directors and large service companies already speak to the family about one contract, and Closure uses that contact to offer the rest. The one-in-four figure is hers, from 2023, and the checkout price now charged to families was not the model in that interview.

competitors.difference: Unlike BYOND, where a person stores accounts for family to open after a death, Closure contacts the companies and asks them to end or transfer the contracts.

entries.research_summary: Digital legacy and estate-planning product for documenting wishes and assets for heirs.
entries.job: Eterny keeps a household's bank accounts, insurance, home, crypto and papers in one private place, and warns about renewals, a blank beneficiary or cover that no longer matches the home. You choose who can open it, and when. The terms, from Eterny Legacy s.r.o. in Bystřice pod Hostýnem, describe it as a place for assets, wills and the people allowed to receive them. The site says files are encrypted on the phone before they are uploaded.
entries.who_pays: The household pays. The site says documents, trusted contacts and one connected bank stay free, including if you stop paying, and that you pay for the gap-checking and for extra banks. Apple lists Eterny Premium at 199 Czech koruna a month or 1,990 Czech koruna a year.

what_it_does.text: Eterny keeps a household's bank accounts, insurance, home, crypto and papers in one private place, and warns about renewals, a blank beneficiary or cover that no longer matches the home. You choose who can open it, and when. The terms, from Eterny Legacy s.r.o. in Bystřice pod Hostýnem, describe it as a place for assets, wills and the people allowed to receive them. The site says files are encrypted on the phone before they are uploaded.

who_pays.text: The household pays. The site says documents, trusted contacts and one connected bank stay free, including if you stop paying, and that you pay for the gap-checking and for extra banks. Apple lists Eterny Premium at 199 Czech koruna a month or 1,990 Czech koruna a year.

traction.text: The about page says 17,000 households in the EU and the US use Eterny, and that the checking has looked at more than 100,000 assets. Apple shows 4.6 out of 5 from 9 ratings. A review dated 29 January 2026 called the app early, and the developer replied on 5 February 2026 that it was still in beta.

why_interesting.text: The free record and the family's access stay open if you cancel. You lose the warnings, not the papers. That is a different bet from a storage app that locks heirs out when the subscription ends. The 17,000 household figure is the company's own, next to nine public app ratings.

status.text: As of 5 October 2026 Eterny is on the Apple App Store, with version 2.15.0 listed on 25 September, after a 31 December 2025 build. The terms took effect on 1 December 2025.

status.text: The site takes requests on weekdays from 08:00 to 16:00 and names Jonas Behrend and Jamie Hartmann as managers. The January 2022 report said Inqbaker would keep the name. No news found in the last 12 months.

traction.text: Antonia Albert and her brother Nikolaus Albert founded Careship in Berlin in 2015 after their grandmother needed help. She studied business administration in the Netherlands and Switzerland and worked at Rocket Internet. The site says more than 150,000 visits and a Google rating of 4.4 out of 5. Care Inside reported on 31 January 2022 that they had raised 13 million euro, filed for insolvency in December 2021, and that Inqbaker would continue the firm from 1 February 2022 with more than 1,600 helpers.

who_pays.text: Families request the visits. Care insurance can be billed under sections 36, 39, and 45b of SGB XI, and a health insurer can pay household help under sections 38 and 24h of SGB V. Private customers file the invoice themselves. No public price. The sale is a direct request, and insurance or private pay can apply.

what_it_does.text: Careship finds a local helper for housework, company, and daily tasks. A person calls or sends a request, agrees the tasks, and starts without a long contract. The site says the same helper returns. Care Companion GmbH places self-employed helpers, and Careship Ambulant GmbH uses employed ones.

why_interesting.text: The insurer can be the payer, and the offer is one returning helper. The 2026 site still takes requests and names Jonas Behrend and Jamie Hartmann as managers rather than the founding siblings.

competitors.difference: Unlike Pflege.de, which publishes care guides and ships supply boxes, Careship sends a helper into the home.

competitors.difference: Compared with AIUDO, which handles payroll when a Spanish family employs the carer, Careship can bill German insurers.

traction.text: The history page says that in 2023 more than 200 people with spinal cord injury tested it and walked more than 400,000 steps.  The company closed a 704,000 euro pre-seed round in 2019. EIT said the consortium received 2.8 million euros between 2020 and 2022. Carnicero said a further 850,000 euro round closed in 2023.

who_pays.text: Hospitals, clinics, and neurological rehabilitation centres are the buyers. The company sells directly in Spain and through distributors in Italy and Poland. No public price. what_it_does.text: ABLE Human Motion sells the ABLE Exoskeleton, a light device for rehabilitation clinics. It helps people practise standing and walking. The history page dates a CE mark for clinical use to 2024. Clinics use the wearable device for gait training.

why_interesting.text: Alfons Carnicero co-founded the company in October 2018 with engineering classmate Alex Garcia and mechanical engineering professor Josep M Font, as a spin-off of Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya. Genesis Biomed says Carnicero holds a master's degree in industrial engineering from UPC and started his career at Implantcast and Institut Guttmann. The clinic device is not sold as a wheelchair replacement.

traction.text: The about page says more than 100 employees, more than 400 guides and magazine pieces, and more than 30,000 readers a day. why_interesting.text: The free guides are the front door. The history page dates the company to 2011, while the homepage says Lars Kilchert and Benedikt Zacher founded it in 2012.

entries.title: Helpper
entries.research_summary: an online platform connecting neighbors for home assistance services in a flexible and easy way.
entries.job: Helpper connects people in Flanders and Brussels who need a hand at home with neighbours who have been screened. The tasks are ordinary, not medical: cooking, shopping, small jobs, a lift to an appointment, company, or keeping an eye on someone. Older people use it to stay in their own home, and a family can also pay a relative who already helps. Helpers are at least 16, and the visits are insured with AG Insurance.
entries.who_pays: The person asking for help pays the helper's hourly rate. On the page for older people, a 3-month membership is €14.99 a month and a 12-month membership is €9.99 a month, with no service fee. Without a membership that page adds a 20% service fee, plus 21% VAT on the fee. People with a Flemish disability budget (PVB or PAB) can set the hourly rate up to €50 and pay a 12% service fee plus 21% VAT. A worked example is 10 hours at €15, which comes to €171.78.

what_it_does.text: Helpper connects people in Flanders and Brussels who need a hand at home with neighbours who have been screened. The tasks are ordinary, not medical: cooking, shopping, small jobs, a lift to an appointment, company, or keeping an eye on someone. Older people use it to stay in their own home, and a family can also pay a relative who already helps. Helpers are at least 16, and the visits are insured with AG Insurance.

who_pays.text: The person asking for help pays the helper's hourly rate. On the page for older people, a 3-month membership is €14.99 a month and a 12-month membership is €9.99 a month, with no service fee. Without a membership that page adds a 20% service fee, plus 21% VAT on the fee. People with a Flemish disability budget (PVB or PAB) can set the hourly rate up to €50 and pay a 12% service fee plus 21% VAT. A worked example is 10 hours at €15, which comes to €171.78.

traction.text: Helpper says it has more than 7,000 screened helpers in Flanders and Brussels. Belgian filings for 2025 show 14.6 full-time staff, a gross margin of €2,603,104 and a profit of €1,408,987. Those accounts were filed on 17 June 2026, and the registry lists the company as active.

why_interesting.text: A family can pay a neighbour, or a relative they already know, for ordinary help, and people with a Flemish disability budget can use that budget for the same thing. The Belgian state recognises Helpper for its sharing-economy tax rules, so the pay is declared rather than handed over in cash. The helper can earn up to €7,890 gross this way in 2026 before a higher tax rate applies.

status.text: The website is taking registrations, and the Belgian registry lists Helpper as active with a 2025 balance sheet filed on 17 June 2026.

entries.job: Momo Medical puts a sensor under a nursing-home mattress and links it to an app on the night shift. entries.who_pays: Nursing homes pay a subscription that covers the app, the bed sensors, and the network linking them. No monthly price is published. The company offers a care location three months of the app at no charge.

what_it_does.text: Momo Medical puts a sensor under a nursing-home mattress and links it to an app on the night shift. Staff can see who is restless, who is still showing signs of life, and who is about to get out of bed. The company says a personal alert can come up to 70 seconds before a resident leaves the bed. Homes use it so staff skip rounds for people who are sleeping safely.

who_pays.text: Nursing homes pay a subscription that covers the app, the bed sensors, and the network linking them. No monthly price is published. The company offers a care location three months of the app at no charge.

traction.text: The company's NPEX page says more than 300 Dutch nursing homes use BedSense, plus dozens of homes in North America, Germany, and Belgium, and more than 20,000 residents. Subscriptions passed 14,000 by the end of 2024. Net sales were 2,070,105 euros in 2023, 3,990,659 euros in 2024, and 3,008,600 euros in the first half of 2025. Named users include tanteLouise, which has used it for six years, plus Laurens, Surplus, Allevo, Attent, and UMC Pitman. The NPEX page says falls fell by 28 percent. That figure is the company's own.

why_interesting.text: Sales almost doubled from 2023 to 2024, but the company was still losing money: 1,502,726 euros after tax in 2024 and 699,623 euros in the first half of 2025. In September 2024 it raised 6.5 million euros from PGGM, NextGen Venture, Jay Searson, UNETI Ventures, and the Centre for Aging + Brain Health Innovation, and said it wanted to reach 30,000 beds in Dutch nursing care.

status.text: The product site is taking trial requests, Y Combinator marks the company active, and the NPEX page still publishes results through 30 June 2025. Momo Medical was founded in Delft in 2017 by Menno Gravemaker.

entries.title: Livy Care - HUM Systems
entries.research_summary: The Operating System for Patient Monitoring.
entries.job: Livy Care, made by HUM Systems, is a sensor fixed to the ceiling of a room in a care home or hospital. It notices a fall, a spoken call for help, and warning signs such as sitting on the edge of the bed or getting up, then alerts the nurse. The person does not wear a device or press a button. It can also file blood pressure, pulse, oxygen, weight, blood sugar and detected falls into the care record.
entries.who_pays: Care home groups and hospitals pay. The price is hardware per room, a software licence per sensor, plus setup, training and support, and it depends on how many rooms are fitted and which functions are switched on. No public unit price is listed.

what_it_does.text: Livy Care, made by HUM Systems, is a sensor fixed to the ceiling of a room in a care home or hospital. It notices a fall, a spoken call for help, and warning signs such as sitting on the edge of the bed or getting up, then alerts the nurse. The person does not wear a device or press a button. It can also file blood pressure, pulse, oxygen, weight, blood sugar and detected falls into the care record.

who_pays.text: Care home groups and hospitals pay. The price is hardware per room, a software licence per sensor, plus setup, training and support, and it depends on how many rooms are fitted and which functions are switched on. No public unit price is listed.

traction.text: The company names users including Johannesstift Diakonie, ProCurand, Johanniter senior houses, AWO NOW, Stiftung Kreuznacher Diakonie, Seniorenzentren Linz, Asklepios, MEDICLIN, Klinikum Frankfurt (Oder), GPR Klinikum, St. Marienstift Friesoythe and the von Bodelschwingh foundations Bethel. A study by FH Oberösterreich reported routine checks falling from about 44 hours a week to 19. A University of Bielefeld study reported about 30% less felt workload for staff. Seniorenzentren Linz reported 34% less time on vital signs and 93.63 staff hours saved in a month.

why_interesting.text: A button alarm fails when the person cannot press it, which is common after a fall or in dementia. Livy watches the room instead. The company also says it does not meet the German nurse-call standard DIN VDE 0834, so where that standard is required the sensor sits beside the existing call system rather than replacing it. HUM Systems started with a ceiling smoke alarm sold with Vattenfall, more than 70,000 units, and later turned the same idea toward care.

status.text: The product site is live and lists trade events in October and November 2026, including IFAS in Zurich and the German nursing congress in Berlin. HUM Systems describes itself as based in Berlin, with development in Berlin and Brandenburg.

entries.job: Jubenial lists Spanish homes for owners over 65 who want cash without moving out. In a bare-ownership sale, the owner sells the title and keeps the right to live in the home for life, with no loan and no monthly repayments. The site also lists lifetime-rent deals and small co-investment stakes in housing for older people, and it shows buyers an expected return on each listing. A valuation is free, and nothing is signed until the owner accepts an offer.
entries.who_pays: The older owner is the seller. The buyer is an investor who waits to take full ownership when the lifetime right to live there ends. Jubenial does not publish a fee. A homepage listing showed a flat in Gijón at 157,500 euros against a stated market value of 260,000 euros. The cash the owner receives depends on the home's value and on age.

traction.text: El Referente, updated 11 September 2025, says the project started in August 2023, put out a first version in January 2024, and raised a 100,000 euro pre-seed round in March 2024, after time in La Finca Ventures Camp. The same profile says 2024 revenue beat the first-year plan by more than 76 percent, and it reports a positive result above 40,000 euros on the profit measure it labels EBITDA, and it lists a 2025 company value of 2 million euros. Those figures are from that startup profile, not from accounts I could read. EntreMayores named Rodolfo Nevado and Víctor Tostado as the founders in an 18 October 2024 article.

why_interesting.text: The older the resident, the less the lifetime right to stay is valued, and the more cash the sale pays now. Heirs do not receive the home. They receive whatever money is left. EntreMayores, quoting Nevado, still called lifetime rent and reverse mortgages a small share of Spanish home sales, even as the company builds a list around them.

status.text: The site is listing homes and inviting free valuations. El Referente marked the company open in its 11 September 2025 update, with an address in Pozuelo de Alarcón, Madrid.

traction.text: Cursor says Rick and Vincent studied industrial design at Eindhoven University of Technology. Eindhoven University of Technology says the compass was invented by Professor Rens Brankaert and developed with 100 people with dementia. On 9 April 2025 Cursor quoted Rick Eurlings on a test of almost 40 people with more advanced dementia, of whom only two or three had trouble finding the way back. No funding round was found.

who_pays.text: The person or family pays 24.99 euro a month, which includes the compass, the connection, and the location app. The subscription can be cancelled monthly. The first two months can be returned for a refund of the money paid, minus shipping, handling, and any damage. Orders now reserve a compass for December 2026. Private pay. No insurance route was found.

what_it_does.text: Aumens sells Het Kompas, a device that points toward home after someone presses a button at the front door. An app shows carers where the compass is. It was designed with people in the early and middle stages of dementia. Rick and Vincent Eurlings founded the company at the end of 2023.

why_interesting.text: The main job is an arrow the person follows, with GPS as a backup for the carer. On 23 March 2026 ONS Magazine described the same device and called the brothers product developers. The site is still taking reservations for delivery at the end of December 2026.

entries.name: Ally Labs
entries.summary: Listens in care-home bedrooms and alerts staff at night.

scene.job: It is a smart home.

deep_dive.product: A smart home.

entries.title: Ally Labs
entries.research_summary: a smart home.
entries.job: Ally puts a Wi-Fi monitor in a care-home bedroom. It uses sound and motion to separate a resident's activity from ordinary background noise, then alerts staff in an app when someone calls for help, gets up, seems restless, or may be in discomfort. Teams use it at night so they can answer those alerts instead of walking in for routine checks. The Local Government Association says the sensor builds a behaviour profile over about two weeks, and homes are told to switch it off during the day.
entries.who_pays: Care homes are the buyer. Ally does not publish a list price. It says homes typically see a 7x return, and the site has a calculator based on bed count and the night-check schedule. In Dorset, the Digitising Social Care programme funded the pilot. Ally's own account of that programme says each participating home received £10,000.

status.text: Companies House lists Ally Labs Limited as active, with accounts made up to 31 August 2025, at Naldretts Court, Wisborough Green. The product site was still selling the bedroom monitor. No news found in the last 12 months.

traction.text: On 3 February 2025 the Local Government Association wrote that six Dorset homes were due to receive 184 Ally sensors. Ally's site cites research claiming 63 percent fewer bedroom falls. Companies House incorporated Ally Labs Limited on 10 November 2015. No funding round was found.

Goldman previously managed products at Google, and Directr, a company he started, was acquired by YouTube, while Rovak was previously chief executive of Fahrenheit 212, which Capgemini acquired. entries.job: CARU care is a home emergency alarm from CARU AG in Zurich. A person can call for help with a wrist or neck button, with a fall sensor in that button, or by saying help. The base unit can also remind someone to drink and to open a window when the air is stuffy. It connects over the mobile network or Wi-Fi to an alarm centre.
entries.who_pays: Care organisations install it and connect it to their own alarm centre. CARU says people with a recognised care grade in Germany get the same care-fund subsidy as a standard home alarm, €27 including VAT. The device is listed in the German care-aid directory as number 52.40.01.1116.

what_it_does.text: CARU care is a home emergency alarm from CARU AG in Zurich. A person can call for help with a wrist or neck button, with a fall sensor in that button, or by saying help. The base unit can also remind someone to drink and to open a window when the air is stuffy. It connects over the mobile network or Wi-Fi to an alarm centre.

who_pays.text: Care organisations install it and connect it to their own alarm centre. CARU says people with a recognised care grade in Germany get the same care-fund subsidy as a standard home alarm, €27 including VAT. The device is listed in the German care-aid directory as number 52.40.01.1116.

traction.text: CARU names deployments with Volkssolidarität Chemnitz, the German Red Cross in Paderborn, and the Bavarian Red Cross in Erding and Würzburg. The company says 90% of users turn on fall detection and 80% use a health reminder. The Swiss register still shows the company at Weberstrasse 3 in Zurich, with a capital update on 9 December 2025.

why_interesting.text: A classic home alarm does nothing if the person cannot reach the button. CARU adds a fall sensor and a spoken call, and the German care-aid list accepted the device in July 2022 as a home alarm that works over a mobile SIM or a home router. It is a box in the house, not software for running a care home.

status.text: The product site is live, and the Swiss commercial register shows CARU AG still seated in Zurich, with a statute and capital filing on 9 December 2025.

entries.title: Essence SmartCare
entries.research_summary: Radar-based indoor fall detector (MDsense) that works without a wearable, sold with Care@Home PERS systems.
entries.job: Essence SmartCare sells MDsense, a wall-mounted radar that looks for a fall indoors and does not need the person to wear a pendant. The product page says it works in the dark, can be used near bathing areas, tells people from pets up to 30 kilograms, and covers a room of up to 4 by 4 metres. It is meant to connect to the company's Care@Home alarm service for homes and senior residences. A 2020 launch notice says the sensor has no video and no sound.
entries.who_sells: Used by seniors at home and retirement facilities.
entries.who_pays: The pages describe MDsense for independent living and for senior care facilities, sold with Care@Home to care providers. No public unit price was found.

what_it_does.text: Essence SmartCare sells MDsense, a wall-mounted radar that looks for a fall indoors and does not need the person to wear a pendant. The product page says it works in the dark, can be used near bathing areas, tells people from pets up to 30 kilograms, and covers a room of up to 4 by 4 metres. It is meant to connect to the company's Care@Home alarm service for homes and senior residences. A 2020 launch notice says the sensor has no video and no sound.

who_pays.text: The pages describe MDsense for independent living and for senior care facilities, sold with Care@Home to care providers. No public unit price was found.

traction.text: Essence SmartCare announced MDsense on 11 September 2020 and said its own research found that less than half of people in residential care wear a fall detector. In June 2021 the product won Connected World's IoT Innovations Award. A later product page says the fall model was trained on more than 20,000 body positions. The parent, Essence Group, said in 2020 that it had 50 million devices deployed. That is a group figure, not a count of MDsense units. The head office is in Herzliya, Israel, with offices in London, Hoboken, and Madrid.

why_interesting.text: A pendant only helps if the person is wearing it, and Essence says fewer than half of residential-care residents do. The radar watches the room instead, without a camera. The published coverage is only 4 by 4 metres, so each room that should be watched, including the bathroom, needs its own sensor.

status.text: The MDsense product page is still published, and the contact page lists a head office in Herzliya plus offices in the UK, the US, and Spain. Essence SmartCare is part of Essence Group.

entries.job: The watch carries its own 4G SIM, so it needs no phone and no wifi. Holding the button for three seconds sends an SOS. If an accelerometer sees a sudden movement or impact, the watch vibrates, beeps, and counts down. The wearer can cancel by holding the button. Otherwise the Family plan calls relatives, and the Professional plan calls Eulen, which can contact 112. Satellites locate it outdoors. Indoors it uses wifi, which can take a minute and fails underground. Pulse is checked about every 10 minutes. The company says the health numbers are not for diagnosis. Battery life is about four days.
entries.who_pays: The watch is 49 euros, down from 99. Family costs 11.99 euros a month on a yearly bill, or 16.99 month to month. The first year on the yearly plan is 192.90 euros including the watch. There is no lock-in and a one-month return. The Professional plan, with Eulen and a MediQuo chat, has no listed price. The company says more than 30 town halls in Spain, France, and Italy also contract it.

traction.text: In August 2019 the Open University of Catalonia said it had been selling for two months around Barcelona, with 12 staff, a watch, room speakers, and a key fob, from 17 to 45 euros a month. On 4 August 2026 the company said 12,500 families use it. That figure is its own.

why_interesting.text: Public telecare in Spain, in its basic form, is a button in the house. This is the outdoor add-on, and the FAQ says families can keep both. Since 2019 the bundle has shrunk from speakers and a social worker to one watch and the Domio app. The countdown exists because the fall sensor false-alarms, and indoor location is approximate.

status.text: Active in October 2026. The shop and an FAQ dated 13 August 2026 were live, and the blog had posts through 29 September 2026. The consent form names the company SeniorDomo, S.L.

entries.job: easierLife rents alarms for people who want help at the press of a button, at home or outside. A home base, a mobile unit, or a watch can call a professional response centre or the family, and some models add automatic fall detection and GPS. A free app tells relatives when an alarm goes off. The company says the home unit plugs in with no technician, no Wi-Fi, and no home phone, arrives in three to five days, and can be cancelled each month.
entries.who_pays: Private customers pay a monthly fee. The home unit with a response centre is 29.95 euros a month, plus a one-time setup fee of 49.90 euros. With a care grade, the company says the care fund pays 23 euros and easierLife discounts the rest by 6.95 euros, so that home unit costs nothing. The home-and-mobile unit is 44.95 euros a month with a centre, or 19.45 euros after a 25.50 euro care-fund payment. Once a care fund approves the watch, the monthly price falls to 9.45 euros.

entries.research_summary: Hip Guard is a company that specializes in the development and production of an airbag belt designed to protect the hips of seniors.
entries.job: Hip'Guard is a belt with two side airbags for older people at risk of a fall. Sensors watch movement, and the company says a side fall is detected in 0.2 seconds and the airbag on that side inflates in 0.08 seconds, before the person hits the ground. The user guide says it is for daily use at home, in a nursing home, or in a rehab centre, and that it is a poor fit for people who move quickly, because a sudden movement can set it off. Helite, a French airbag maker, builds it. After an inflation, the used gas cartridge has to be replaced.
entries.who_pays: The belt is sold online for 755.24 euros including tax, in five sizes. That price covers the belt, a washable cover, two airbags, two gas generators, and the sensor. A price for the replacement gas cartridge was not listed on the shop page.

founders.name: Gérard Thévenot
founders.role: Founder of Helite, the company that makes Hip'Guard

what_it_does.text: Hip'Guard is a belt with two side airbags for older people at risk of a fall. Sensors watch movement, and the company says a side fall is detected in 0.2 seconds and the airbag on that side inflates in 0.08 seconds, before the person hits the ground. The user guide says it is for daily use at home, in a nursing home, or in a rehab centre, and that it is a poor fit for people who move quickly, because a sudden movement can set it off. Helite, a French airbag maker, builds it. After an inflation, the used gas cartridge has to be replaced.

who_pays.text: The belt is sold online for 755.24 euros including tax, in five sizes. That price covers the belt, a washable cover, two airbags, two gas generators, and the sensor. A price for the replacement gas cartridge was not listed on the shop page.

traction.text: The shop page shows no customer reviews. Hip'Guard says the French lab CRITT found that the belt cuts impact force by 90 percent and absorbs nine times more shock than a standard hip pad, and that UGA tested 828 falls and everyday situations, with the belt firing in 9 of 10 side-fall cases and unwanted firing in 1 percent. Those are the company's reports of the tests. Helite says it now has 45 people and distributors in 50 countries. That is the whole airbag business, not a Hip'Guard sales count.

why_interesting.text: A pendant calls for help after a fall. This belt is meant to soften the blow to the hip. The 90 percent impact claim is large, and it is stated on the maker's own certification page rather than in a paper I could read. The user guide also warns that brisk movement can trigger the airbag, so the people who walk most freely may be the worst fit.

status.text: The belt is for sale on hipguard.eu. The legal notice names HELITE SAS, 1 rue de la petite fin, 21121 Fontaine-lès-Dijon, RCS Dijon 883 586 869, with Gérard Thévenot as publication director. Helite dates its own start to 2002 in Dijon.
